newsitem.title: CANADA: DBRS sees Quebec balanced budget one year late.
newsitem.headline: DBRS sees Quebec balanced budget one year late.

text.p: Dominion Bond Rating Service said on Friday it believed Quebec would take at least one year longer than planned to eliminate its budget deficit.
Canada's largest bond rating agency made the forecast in a study of the economic and fiscal issues facing the French-speaking Canadian province.
"In the opinion of DBRS, Quebec will take at least one additional year to balance its budget compared to its fiscal plan," said a summary of the report.
Quebec officials have pledged to eliminate the province's budget deficit by the 1999-2000 fiscal year.

The Toronto-based bond rating agency said Quebec's fiscal results required "material restatement of reported amounts", including deficit and debt figures, in order to be comparable to other provinces.

The agency said key adjustments included "additional debt from a C$9 billion under accrual of its unfunded pension liabilities; and non-budgetary capital expenditures which typically add C$1 billion to the annual deficit."
DBRS said it retained Quebec's long-term debt rating of A (low) with a negative trend. The agency downgraded the rating in July 1996.

The agency said Quebec's economy had substantial potential and that the province had demonstrated a strong will to address its fiscal problems. DBRS also noted the province had developed a world-class capability in electricity generation, aluminum smelting, mining and forestry.

Factors pressuring the province's fiscal position were the highest deficit relative to gross domestic product in Canada, the second highest debt relative to GDP in Canada, a weakly performing economy with high taxation levels, and declining federal transfers, DBRS said.
Other fiscal issues facing the province included unfunded liabilities related to the Quebec Pension Plan and an aging population, the report said.
The DBRS report noted that Quebec's economic performance lagged behind national averages, with private investment at low levels and a high unemployment rate.

The report also noted that Quebec diversified its sources of capital by accessing several global markets. The province therefore had an above-average level of debt in foreign currencies and a large floating rate exposure.
